title: Black Tie Optional
metaTitle: Black Tie Optional: What It Means for Men and Women
metaDescription: Black tie optional means a tuxedo or a dark suit and tie for men, and a floor-length gown, cocktail dress, LBD or dressy separates for women. Edge cases inside.
h1: Black Tie Optional: What It Means for Men and Women, Case by Case
answer: Black tie optional means the hosts would welcome black tie but will not require it. Men wear a tuxedo, or a dark suit with a white dress shirt, a conservative tie, leather dress shoes and dark socks. Women wear a floor-length gown, a cocktail dress, a little black dress or dressy separates. It is one step below black tie, not a casual code.
intro: Black tie optional is the dress code that causes the most second-guessing, because it gives guests a choice and then leaves them wondering whether the choice was real. It is real. The Emily Post Institute's list allows a tuxedo or a dark suit for men, and four outfits for women, from a floor-length gown to dressy separates. What the word "optional" does not allow is a step below that list: no sport coats, no sundresses, no daytime casual. This page works through the decisions in the order guests face them: what the code means, how it differs from black tie, then the men's and women's choices, then the time, venue and season cases that change the answer.

contentSections.heading: What does black tie optional mean?
contentSections.content:
It means formal evening wear with one built-in alternative for each half of the room. Emily Post's attire guide lists:
• Women: a floor-length gown, a cocktail dress, a little black dress, or dressy separates.
• Men: a tuxedo, or a dark suit with a white dress shirt, a conservative tie, leather dress shoes and dark socks.

The hosts are telling you that tuxedos and gowns are welcome and that you will not be out of place without them. They are not telling you the event is relaxed. The suit option is a dark suit with a tie, and the dress option is a cocktail dress, which is still evening wear.

On a wedding invitation the phrase usually signals a specific kind of day: an evening reception, a seated dinner, often a hotel, ballroom or formal venue, and a wedding party that may itself be in tuxedos and long gowns. The wording lets a couple ask for a formal-looking room without making every guest rent a tuxedo or buy a gown. Your job as a guest is to land anywhere on the list and look as though you meant it.

It is also the code guests find hardest to place. Across the 10,700 r/Weddingattireapproval posts we counted (16 April – 21 October 2026; method on our wedding dress code study page), 599 posts, 5.6% of the total, mention black tie optional. The posters themselves file those questions in different places: 369 under Black/White Tie, 138 under Formal, 29 under Special Dress Code and 15 under Cocktail or No Dress Code. If the people asking cannot agree which tier it belongs to, the confusion is in the code, not in you.

contentSections.heading: How it differs from black tie, and from "formal"
contentSections.content:
The table below puts the two codes side by side. For women, the difference is small: black tie optional adds dressy separates and drops the word "dressy" from the cocktail dress. For men, it is the whole question: black tie requires a tuxedo, black tie optional does not.

"Formal" on an evening wedding invitation lands in nearly the same place. Emily Post's wedding-guest page describes formal evening dress as a long evening dress or a dressy cocktail dress for women, depending on local custom, and a tuxedo or a dark suit for men. It adds that a tuxedo becomes required only when the invitation actually says black tie. So if you are deciding between a formal invitation and a black tie optional one, dress for them the same way.

One word of caution: some couples write "black tie optional" while privately hoping for strict black tie. If the wedding website shows a ballroom, an orchestra and a late start, the room will lean toward tuxedos and gowns, and you can match it.

contentSections.heading: Men: choosing between the tuxedo and the dark suit
contentSections.content:
Either is correct, so the decision is about fitting the room rather than meeting a rule. In our dataset, 102 of those 599 posts (17.0%) are about men's attire; 50 mention a tuxedo and 74 mention a suit.

Choose the tuxedo when:
• The wedding starts in the evening, especially after 6 p.m.
• The venue is a ballroom, a hotel, a club or anywhere with a seated dinner and dancing.
• Your partner is wearing a floor-length gown.
• You already own one or are in the wedding party and the couple asks.

Choose the dark suit when:
• The ceremony is in the afternoon.
• The venue is outdoors, rustic or warm.
• You would be renting a tuxedo for one evening and a good suit fits you better.

What counts as a dark suit: Emily Post says dark, and pairs it with a white dress shirt and a conservative tie. Black, charcoal and deep navy all qualify. Mid-gray, light blue, tan, linen and bold patterns do not; they belong to semi-formal or daytime dress. A suit for this code should be a solid or very quiet weave, pressed, with leather dress shoes polished and dark socks.

The tie: Emily Post's word is conservative. Solid, dark, silk. A black bow tie with a dark suit is a choice some men make; it reads as an attempt at a tuxedo, so if you want a bow tie, the tuxedo is the cleaner answer.

If you pick the tuxedo, wear the whole thing: the black bow tie, the studs, the cummerbund or vest. Our black tie attire guide lists every piece. For the men's side of every code, see the wedding dress code for men.

contentSections.heading: Women: gown, cocktail dress or separates
contentSections.content:
Emily Post gives women four options, and all four are fully correct. In our dataset, 140 of the 599 posts (23.4%) mention a gown, a floor-length dress, a maxi or a long dress, while 58 (9.7%) mention a cocktail-length, midi, knee-length or short dress. Long is the more common question, which matches the room you will usually find.

How to decide:
• Floor-length gown: the safest choice for any evening event under this code and the one you can never get wrong.
• Cocktail dress: correct, especially for an afternoon ceremony or a smaller venue. Choose an evening fabric such as satin, crepe, silk or velvet, and a hem at the knee or below. A cocktail dress that would also work at an office party is underdressed here.
• Little black dress: listed by Emily Post. Make it a dressy one, and take care at a daytime ceremony, where an all-black outfit can look severe.
• Dressy separates: a long satin skirt with a silk top, or tailored evening trousers. A jumpsuit counts as dressy separates if the fabric is formal and the cut is polished. A cotton or casual jumpsuit does not.

Cover and comfort matter as much as length. Emily Post's wedding-guest page asks guests to consider whether bare shoulders suit a religious ceremony. Bring a wrap for church, and choose heels that work on the venue's floor. For dresses that match the list, see our black tie optional wedding guest dresses.

contentSections.heading: Time, venue and season change the answer
contentSections.content:
The garment list stays the same, but where you land within it should move with the event.

Daytime. Black tie and its optional version are evening conventions; Wikipedia's Black tie article notes that black tie is traditionally worn after 6 p.m. For an early-afternoon ceremony under this code, lean toward the suit and the cocktail dress. Emily Post's wedding-guest page describes formal daytime dress as a cocktail or dressy afternoon dress for women and a dark suit with a conservative shirt and tie for men.

Evening. After 6 p.m., lean toward the tuxedo and the gown. Neither is required, but they are what most of the room will choose at a late start.

Outdoors. 99 of the 599 posts in our dataset (16.5%) mention an outdoor setting such as a garden, beach, barn or vineyard. Formality does not drop because the venue is a lawn, but practicality rises: a hem that clears the grass, block heels, a wrap for the evening, and for men a suit in a breathable wool.

Summer and heat. Emily Post notes that at black tie, a white dinner jacket with black tuxedo trousers is acceptable in summer, the tropics and on cruises. If you choose a tuxedo for a hot-weather wedding, that is your lighter option.

Religious venues and local custom. Emily Post's wedding-guest page lists bare shoulders, open-toed shoes, head coverings and regional conservatism as things to check. These apply at any formality, but the more formal the event, the more likely the ceremony is in a house of worship.

contentSections.heading: Overdressed or underdressed: which way to lean
contentSections.content:
Lean formal. In our dataset, 37 of the 599 posts (6.2%) worry about being underdressed, against 15 (2.5%) who worry about being overdressed. Guests sense, correctly, that the risk at this code runs one way.

The reasoning is simple. The top of the list, a tuxedo or a floor-length gown, is explicitly welcome, so it cannot be too much. The bottom of the list, a dark suit or a cocktail dress, is explicitly acceptable, so it is not too little. What goes wrong is stepping off the list at the bottom: a blazer and chinos, a light summer suit, a sundress, a day dress in cotton.

If you are in a couple, the two of you do not need to match tier for tier, but a pairing that spans the list looks odd: a floor-length beaded gown next to a gray suit and no tie, or a tuxedo next to a casual midi. Aim for the same end of the list.

When in doubt about one item, pick the dressier version of it: the darker suit, the silk tie instead of the knit one, the satin cocktail dress instead of the crepe day dress.

contentSections.heading: Still unsure? Work through it in this order
contentSections.content:
Most questions about this code resolve in four steps:
• Read the time. After 6 p.m., lean tuxedo and gown; before, lean suit and cocktail dress.
• Read the venue. A ballroom or hotel pulls formal; a garden, barn or beach pulls practical, not casual.
• Read the wedding website. Couples often explain the dress code there, and photos of the venue tell you a lot.
• Ask. A short message to the couple or someone in the wedding party is normal and appreciated, and it is the only way to know whether "optional" was a polite way of saying black tie.

The mistakes guests most often make with this code:
• Reading "optional" as "no dress code."
• Wearing a light or patterned suit because a suit is allowed.
• Pairing a tuxedo with a long necktie, or a suit with a bow tie and calling it black tie.
• A cocktail dress in a daytime fabric.
• White or ivory on a female guest; see our guide to wedding guest dress colors to avoid.

For how this code fits among the others, see our wedding dress codes explained hub, or the black tie attire guide for the stricter version.
